title: What a request is, and p50 versus p99
summary: A request is one question and one answer. Averages hide the slow ones that people remember.

steps.title: One tap, one request
steps.text: A request is one question from a person ("show my feed") and one answer. Every request waits a little. Latency is that wait, in milliseconds (ms). A blink is about 100 ms (approx.).

steps.title: p50 and p99
steps.text: p50 is the wait that half of requests beat, the typical one. p99 is the wait that 99 of every 100 requests beat, so the slowest 1 in 100 is slower than that. If a page makes 10 requests, about 1 page in 10 meets a p99 request, so p99 is what people feel.

steps.prompt: People in Europe wait too long. Follow the whole request path: move both the app servers and their database to Europe so no request crosses the ocean.
steps.hint: Select the server and the database, then set Region to Europe. The trip across the ocean and back adds about 80 ms (approx.).

rows.label: Europe to Asia Pacific and back

choices: The average wait across every request
The wait the fastest 1 in 100 saw
The wait of the single slowest request
steps.why: The slowest 1 in 100 requests is slower than p99.

steps.q: Why watch p99 and not just the average?
choices: The p99 is far cheaper to measure
A few very slow requests spoil a page
The average is always wrong by half
Users only ever read the p99 figure
steps.why: A page makes many requests, so slow ones show up often for real people.

steps.q: How do you cut the wait for far-away users?
choices: Add more memory to every server
Turn off all logging for a day
Put the service closer to them
steps.why: Distance sets a floor on latency that no faster server can beat.

takeaway: Judge a system by its slow requests, and remember distance is part of latency.
